proposed.text: A building owner compares two escalator specifications for a new shopping center: Option A (800 mm step width, 30 m/min, 30 deg inclination) vs. Option B (1000 mm step width, 38 m/min rated-speed limit, 35 deg maximum inclination). What are the implications of choosing Option B?

options.text: Option B provides higher capacity with minimal additional cost; always preferred for commercial projects

Option B provides higher theoretical capacity but requires enhanced safety systems, higher motor power (kW), stronger structural support, and increased maintenance complexity because it operates at the rated-speed (38 m/min) and inclination (35 deg) limits
Option B reduces energy consumption by using maximum inclination; it is more efficient than Option A
Option B is identical in safety profile to Option A; the choice depends only on aesthetic preferences

proposed.rationale: Option B (1000 mm, 38 m/min rated-speed limit, 35 deg maximum inclination) leverages maximum design parameters across width, speed, and inclination. This delivers higher capacity but demands enhanced safety systems (reinforced balustrades, stronger emergency stops), larger motors, heavier structural loads, and more intensive maintenance because it operates at the rated-speed and inclination limits. The original 0.5 m/s / 0.65 m/s speed bases have been replaced with the article body's 38 m/min basis for a single consistent speed basis. Source: Salvan Architectural Utilities 2 (escalator rated speed max 38 m/min along the incline; inclination max 35 deg).
